choices: The team identified too many stakeholders, which diluted their effort
Power and interest shift over time, so the assessment must be repeated; the single kickoff score became out of date
The board's interest was overstated, so the team wasted effort on it
The team should have placed the board in the low-interest, low-power quadrant from the start
questions.why: The teaching text warns that power and interest change when conditions change, such as a permit refusal, so a one-time assessment becomes stale.

questions.prompt: On a port terminal expansion, a sponsor's team in one region expects bad news to be delivered in person before it appears in any written report, while a second team expects a detailed written answer first. What should the project manager do with this difference?
choices: Send all bad news in writing only, since written records are always safest
Pick one style for all stakeholders so the reporting stays consistent
Record each group's communication preference in the stakeholder register and match the message to how that group reads it
Skip the in-person delivery because relationship habits do not belong in project records
questions.why: The teaching text says culture-based communication preferences are recorded in the register so messages match how each group reads them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which stakeholders get the most of your time on a construction project, and name one limit of the power/interest method that you would watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from a full stakeholder register so nobody is left off, then score each person on power and interest and place them on a power/interest grid. High power and high interest people get close, frequent contact, such as the owner's representative and the general contractor's superintendent. High power but lower interest, like a building inspector, get scheduled milestone notices so they are never surprised. High interest but low power, such as neighbours affected by noise, get regular updates so they do not escalate. The limit is that the grid is a snapshot: power and interest shift when a permit is delayed or a complaint lands, so I would rescore at each milestone. The grid also ignores culture, so I would note how each person prefers to receive news and adjust the form of the message, not just the frequency.
rubricPoints: Defines a stakeholder as anyone who can affect or is affected by the project, and says identification comes before assessment
Explains power and interest as the two assessment measures and how they map to engagement effort
Names at least one limit, such as the grid being a snapshot that goes stale or ignoring cultural preferences
Shows that the register records communication preferences so messages match how each stakeholder reads them

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying who gets attention is best learned by explaining the reasoning back, since no listed mission or planned engine covers stakeholder assessment.

lessons.plain: Scope is the set of work a project must do to produce what it promised. Defining scope around outcomes and mission means starting from the result the project exists to achieve, such as a clinic that can see more patients by a set date, and then deciding which items are truly needed to reach it. Maturing scope means the early, rough description is sharpened into a detailed, agreed version as the team learns more, and every revision is checked against that original purpose before it is accepted. The skill is keeping the project honest about what it is for, not only about what it builds.
lessons.guessPrompt: A school board asks for a new gym. Before anyone draws anything, what should the project team agree on first, and why might a list of gym features alone be risky?
lessons.teach:
Scope is the total work a project must perform to deliver what it promises. Product scope is the features and qualities of the thing built. Project scope is the work and steps needed to build it. Defining scope well starts with the outcome, meaning the benefit the owner needs once the work is finished, and the mission, meaning the reason the owner is investing at all. Those two anchors tell the team which features are essential and which are nice to have. Scope matures in stages: a broad early statement becomes a detailed scope baseline, which is the agreed version that later work is measured against. Each revision to that baseline should be tested against the outcome and recorded with approval, so the team knows what changed and why.

Worked example. A rural clinic plans a new treatment room so that 30 patients a day can be seen by September. The first scope says build one room with two beds. A survey then shows the room must also meet an accessibility requirement, so a level entrance is added. Step one: check the outcome. Thirty patients a day still needs a waiting area sized for them, which the first scope never included. Step two: add the waiting area to the scope, record the revision with its reason, and get the owner's sign-off. Step three: update the baseline so the contractor prices from current drawings.

Common mistake: listing deliverables without the outcome, so a complete-looking scope still fails the clinic. Consequence: the room is built on time but cannot handle the patient load, and the owner pays again.

A scope is accurate only when every item traces back to an outcome the owner has agreed to.

questions.prompt: A regional sports federation needs a new indoor hall that can host 200-spectator tournaments by March. The first scope includes one indoor court only. A fire-safety review then requires seating for 200 people and a second exit. Step one: check the outcome. Seating and a second exit are needed for the tournaments to go ahead legally, so both belong in scope. Step two: [missing]. Step three: update the scope baseline so the contractor prices from current drawings. Which action correctly fills the missing step two?
choices: Price the added seating from the original one-court estimate and start work before sign-off.
Remove the seating from scope because the first scope never mentioned it.
Add the seating and second exit to the scope, record the revision with its reason, and get the owner's sign-off.
Ask the contractor to build the seating as an optional extra after the hall opens.
questions.why: Step two is where each revision is added to the scope, recorded with its reason, and approved by the owner, which is what keeps the scope traceable to the outcome.

questions.prompt: A water utility's team has a list of pipes, valves and pumps for a pumping station, but no statement of the service the station must provide. What is the main risk of this scope?
choices: Items may be built on time, but the service need is unverified, so scope is inaccurate.
Later revisions can add the missing outcome when asked, so no check is needed now.
The items count as product scope, so project scope is automatically correct for the owner.
The team can skip recording changes since the list already looks complete and finished.
questions.why: A scope is accurate only when every item traces back to an outcome the owner has agreed to, and a list with no outcome can be fully built yet still fail the owner's need.

questions.prompt: A hospital car park expansion's first scope adds 120 spaces. A later review shows the outcome needs 40 of those spaces reserved for staff with mobility needs, placed near the entrance. Which action best fits the scope-revision approach?
choices: Add the reserved spaces, get owner approval, then update the baseline.
Keep 120 and let the contractor pick the reserved layout during construction.
Cut the total to 80 so the baseline does not change at all.
Note the reserved spaces on the drawing only, leaving the scope and baseline unchanged.
questions.why: The reserved spaces are a new requirement that the outcome depends on, so they must be added to scope, approved by the owner, and then reflected in the baseline.

questions.prompt: A team adds a feature to a school kitchen project but never records the reason for the change or who approved it. Six months later, nobody can explain a cost rise. What is the core failure?
choices: Any feature added later becomes part of the outcome automatically, so no approval is needed at all.
Revisions lacked a recorded reason and approval, so changes cannot be traced to an agreed outcome.
The baseline should have stayed as the early broad statement so later changes would be easier to hide from the owner.
The contractor must have priced the work wrongly, so this is a pricing failure rather than a scope failure.
questions.why: Each revision must be tested against the outcome and recorded with approval, and without that record the team cannot show what changed or why.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would define a project's scope from its outcome and mission, and how you would revise that scope as the design matures. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking the owner what result they need once the work is done and why the project matters to them. That outcome and mission become the test for every feature on the list. Then I would write a broad first scope and refine it into a detailed baseline as surveys and designs come in. When something changes, I check whether the revised scope still delivers the agreed outcome, record the reason for the change, and get approval before the baseline is updated. The main limit is that outcomes can be vague, so the team has to pin them down with measurable targets early, or the test becomes a matter of opinion. Also, a tight outcome test can make the team reject useful additions that the owner would have wanted, so the review needs the owner present.
rubricPoints: Scope starts from the owner's outcome and mission, not only from a list of deliverables.
Scope matures from a broad statement into an agreed baseline through stages.
Each revision is tested against the outcome and recorded with a reason and approval.
Names a real limit, such as vague outcomes or the risk of rejecting useful additions.

suggested.rationale: Defining and revising scope against outcomes is a reasoning skill best shown by explaining the approach back to a teammate, and no listed mission or planned engine covers construction scope.

lessons.plain: A change order is a formal, written approval to alter what a construction or capital project will deliver, its cost, or its schedule after the work was agreed. Timing it means deciding when in the project a change is raised and approved, because a change made early costs little while one made late can mean tearing out finished work. Designing the process means deciding who can approve what, how fast, and how the change is recorded, so that a small fix does not wait weeks for a committee while the crew stands idle. Think of it like a permit for a modification: the rules decide when you ask and how quickly you get a yes.
lessons.guessPrompt: On a building site, a wall needs to move 1.5 metres. The crew could make the request during framing, or after the drywall, wiring and inspections are finished. Which is cheaper to change, and why do you think so?
lessons.teach:
A change order is a formal written instruction that alters the agreed scope, cost or schedule of a project after a baseline has been approved. The baseline is the agreed version of scope, cost and schedule that everyone measures progress against. A change control process is the set of steps for raising, assessing, approving and recording a change. The cost of a change rises as work progresses, because each completed stage adds rework, demolition and delay to the change itself. Timing matters for this reason: the earlier a change is raised, the more options remain open and the cheaper it is.

A fast process separates changes by size and risk. Minor changes that fit inside an approved contingency can be approved by the project manager within a set time, such as one working day. Larger changes that affect the critical path, safety or contract value go to a change control board, a small group with authority to approve, reject or defer changes. Agile approaches add short review cycles, such as a weekly board, plus pre-approved limits so routine adjustments do not queue.

Worked example: during framing, the client asks to move a partition wall 1.5 metres. Step one, the project manager logs the request and its reason. Step two, the designer estimates impact: two hours of rework, no effect on the critical path, cost within contingency. Step three, because it is under the threshold, the manager approves it that day and updates the baseline record. Had the same request arrived after drywall, the estimate would include demolition, rewiring and re-inspection, so it would go to the board.

Common mistake: allowing verbal instructions on site to proceed without a written change order. The baseline and cost record then no longer match the work, and the contractor may later dispute payment.

Consequence: an unrecorded change makes schedule and budget reports describe a project that no longer exists, so every later decision is made on wrong information.

questions.prompt: A school extension team is replacing a planned set of aluminium windows with timber-framed windows after the roof is already on. The baseline is the approved version of scope, cost and schedule that progress is measured against, and the contingency is the reserved budget set aside for small unplanned changes. Step 1: the project manager logs the client's request and its reason. Step 2: the architect estimates impact at 1.5 days of rework to remove and refit the frames, a one-day delay to the roof-closure milestone, which sits on the critical path (the chain of tasks that sets the earliest finish date), and a cost of 4% of the contingency. Step 3 is missing: state what happens next and which route the change takes.
choices: The change goes to the change control board because it affects the critical path.
The project manager approves it the same day because the cost is under 5% of the contingency.
The change waits until the final invoice so the cost can be checked against the whole budget.
The architect starts the timber windows on a verbal request and the order is written up at handover.
questions.why: A change that moves the critical path is a larger change that goes to the change control board, regardless of how small its cost is.

questions.prompt: A bridge project's client asks for a new handrail design during the earthworks stage, before any concrete is poured. Another team proposes waiting until the deck is finished. Why is raising the change early generally the better choice?
choices: Because the earlier a change is raised, the more options remain open and the cheaper it tends to be.
Because the change control board meets only during earthworks and is unavailable later.
Because a change raised early costs nothing, so there is no reason to estimate it.
Because the baseline is only approved after the deck is complete, so earlier requests are not yet valid.
questions.why: The teaching text says cost rises as work progresses since each completed stage adds rework, demolition and delay, so early raising keeps options open and lowers cost.

questions.prompt: A warehouse fit-out has a contingency of 10,000 currency units. A tenant requests a relocated light switch that costs 4,000, adds no time to the critical path, has no safety effect, and does not change the contract value. Under a fast change process, which route fits best?
choices: The tenant decides alone, since tenants can approve changes to their own space.
The project manager approves it within the set time, because it is a minor change that fits inside the approved contingency.
The site foreman approves it verbally and the written order is raised at month end.
The change goes to a weekly board and waits for the next meeting before any work starts.
questions.why: A minor change that fits inside an approved contingency and does not touch the critical path, safety or contract value is approved by the project manager within the set time.

questions.prompt: On a hospital wing, a site engineer agrees a change to ceiling heights with a subcontractor by phone and tells them to start. The written change order is not raised until two weeks later. What is the most likely consequence for the project records?
choices: The schedule is automatically corrected by the critical path software, so no record is needed.
The change control board will approve the change retroactively with no further cost impact.
The baseline and cost record no longer match the work actually done, and the contractor may later dispute payment.
The project has no problem, because the verbal instruction was given by a qualified engineer.
questions.why: Work proceeding without a written change order leaves the baseline and cost record out of step with the work, which can lead to a payment dispute with the contractor.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a change order should be raised as early as possible, and name one tradeoff of making the approval process faster.
lessons.modelAnswer: Raising a change early is cheaper because little work has been built on the old design, so there is less rework, demolition and delay to pay for, and more alternatives remain open. A late change can force us to undo finished stages. The tradeoff of speeding up approval is control: if a site manager can approve small changes in a day, several small changes can add up to a large cost or schedule shift that nobody with budget authority has reviewed. So I would set a value and schedule threshold, keep a weekly board for anything larger, and require a written record for every change, even fast ones, so the baseline stays accurate.
rubricPoints: Explains that change cost rises as construction progresses, so earlier raising is cheaper
Describes tiering: small changes approved quickly within limits, larger ones to a board
Names a real tradeoff of faster approval, such as cumulative unreviewed impact
Notes that every change, fast or slow, must be recorded against the baseline

suggested.rationale: Timing and tiering a change process is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style scenario about when and how to approve a change, and no listed mission covers construction change orders.

lessons.plain: A scope change is any addition, removal or alteration to what a project will deliver. Evaluating a scope change against core project outcomes means asking a plain question before saying yes: does this change still help the project achieve what it was built to achieve? Those outcomes usually include the facility's purpose, its budget limit, its completion date, and its quality and safety standards. Technology-assisted change management uses shared software to log requests, route them for approval, track costs and keep one record of decisions. That speeds things up and reduces lost paperwork, but the software only records decisions. It cannot decide whether a change is worth making, and a tidy approval workflow can hide weak thinking.
lessons.guessPrompt: A client asks to add a second loading dock to a warehouse midway through construction. The schedule has two weeks of spare time before the finish date, and the budget has a small reserve. What would you check before approving it, and why would a completed approval in the software not be enough on its own?
lessons.teach:
Scope is the set of work and deliverables a project commits to. Core outcomes are the reasons the project exists, such as its purpose, cost, completion date, quality and safety. A change request is a formal proposal to alter scope. A change order is the approved, written record that changes the scope, cost or time. An impact assessment is the analysis of what a proposed change does to cost, schedule, risk and quality. Float is spare time in the schedule before a delay moves the finish date. Contingency is a reserve of money set aside for unknowns. A technology-assisted process is a shared tool that routes requests for approval, keeps an audit trail and links to cost and schedule data.

Why evaluate against outcomes? Every change is judged by what it does to the reason the project exists, not only by whether someone wants it. Worked example: the dock adds 48,000 in cost against a 60,000 reserve, and takes 9 working days of work that fits inside the 10 days of float. Step 1: restate the outcome, which is that the warehouse opens on time at its target throughput. Step 2: check cost, which fits the reserve. Step 3: check schedule, which holds only if the dock work sits in float. Step 4: check the benefit, which is the throughput the client needs. Step 5: check hidden effects, such as whether the crane booking that the dock work needs is already committed elsewhere. The software will show the estimate and approval, but not the crane conflict unless someone enters it.

Common mistake: treating a complete workflow as proof of a sound evaluation, or approving each small change against the reserve without adding up their combined effect. In a running project, that leads to the reserve being spent while the record still shows green, and the outcome drifts without anyone seeing it.

A change is sound only when its effect on the project's outcomes has been assessed, and the tool records that assessment rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: A school extension team is assessing change request CR-7, which adds an acoustic wall upgrade costing 35,000. A change request is a formal proposal to alter scope. The project's contingency, a reserve of money set aside for unknowns, holds 40,000. The upgrade takes 6 working days, and the schedule has 4 days of float, meaning spare time before a delay moves the finish date. The core outcome is that classrooms open for the September term at the agreed acoustic standard. Worked so far: Step 1, restate the outcome as classrooms open for September at the agreed acoustic standard. Step 2, check cost: 35,000 fits within the 40,000 contingency. Step 4, check benefit: the acoustic standard is a stated requirement of the school. Step 3, check schedule, is the missing step. Which completion of Step 3 is correct?
choices: The work fits, because 6 days is close to 4 days and small overruns are normally absorbed.
The schedule check is unnecessary, because an upgrade is not new scope.
The 6 days exceed the 4 days of float by 2 days, so the finish date is at risk unless the work is resequenced or float is recovered.
The schedule check is passed because the cost is within the contingency.
questions.why: Float covers only 4 days, so 6 days of work pushes the finish date unless the work is reorganised, and cost fitting the contingency says nothing about time.

questions.prompt: A project team needs a written analysis of what a proposed change does to cost, schedule, risk and quality before deciding whether to approve it. Which term names that analysis?
choices: Contingency
Change order
Impact assessment
Change request
questions.why: An impact assessment is the analysis of a change's effect on cost, schedule, risk and quality; a change request is the proposal, a change order is the approved record, and contingency is a money reserve.

questions.prompt: A clinic renovation has 14 small changes, each approved after being checked alone against the remaining 50,000 contingency. Each one fit on its own, but together they total 62,000, and the approval tool shows every item as green. What is the core failure?
choices: The tool logged the approvals, so the outcome is protected.
The contingency is the wrong size for a clinic project.
The tool did not show the changes at all.
Each change was checked alone, and the combined total against the reserve was never added up.
questions.why: Approving each change against the reserve separately hides their combined effect, so the 62,000 total overspends the 50,000 reserve while the record still looks clean.

questions.prompt: A shared approval tool shows a change order as approved, with a full audit trail and linked cost data. The change needs a concrete pump truck that is already booked for another job, and nobody entered that booking in the tool. What does the approved status tell you?
choices: That the workflow was completed, but the hidden resource conflict was not captured.
That the change has no effect on the schedule.
That the audit trail is incomplete and the change should be reversed.
That the effects on the project's outcomes, including the pump truck conflict, were assessed.
questions.why: A tool records the workflow and the data entered into it, but it does not detect a conflict unless someone enters it, so approval alone does not prove the outcome assessment was sound.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a scope change should go ahead, and name one limit of relying on a shared change-order tool to make that decision.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by restating the project outcomes the change could affect: purpose, cost, completion date, quality and safety. Then I assess the change against each one. I estimate its cost and check it against the contingency, check whether its work fits in the float or pushes the finish date, and confirm that the benefit is real. I also look for hidden effects, such as shared resources like cranes or inspectors that other work depends on. The tool is useful because it routes approvals, keeps a record and shows totals. Its limit is that it only holds what people enter. If nobody records the crane conflict or the effect of several small changes added together, the workflow can show an approved, under-budget change while the outcomes quietly drift. So I treat the approval as the end of a judgment I have made, not as the judgment itself.
rubricPoints: Restates the core project outcomes before judging the change
Assesses cost against the contingency, and schedule against float or the finish date
Looks for hidden effects on shared resources or cumulative changes
Names a real limit of the tool, such as it only recording what people enter
Treats an approved workflow as a record of a judgment, not a replacement for it

suggested.rationale: Evaluating a scope change is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers construction scope changes.

lessons.plain: Scope is the agreed set of work a project will deliver. A scope gap is needed work that nobody has planned for, or a requirement the project's outcome depends on but the plan leaves out. Value engineering is a structured review of a design or method that looks for ways to deliver the same needed function at lower cost or with less risk, without dropping what the owner actually needs. Cost-benefit analysis compares what an option costs against the value it returns, so you can decide whether it is worth adding, changing or dropping. Together these tools help a project manager find missing work and decide, with evidence, which gaps to close and how.
lessons.guessPrompt: A building owner says the new clinic must be usable by wheelchair users, but the drawings only show standard doors and a step at the entrance. Before reading anything, how would you decide whether fixing this is worth the extra cost, and what would you need to know first?
lessons.teach:
A scope gap is the distance between what the project must deliver to meet its purpose and what the current scope documents actually cover. Gaps usually appear as requirements stated in the owner's brief that never reached the drawings or specifications, or as functions the design meets only by accident. Value engineering (VE) is a structured review, usually held at a defined design stage, in which the team asks what each element is for and whether the same function can be delivered at lower total cost or lower risk. It is not simply cutting items. A VE idea that removes a required function is a scope reduction and must be handled as one. Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) puts numbers on an option: the cost to add or change it, set against the measurable and non-measurable benefits it returns over the asset's life, such as reduced maintenance, compliance, or avoided rework.

Why it works: the two tools answer different questions. VE asks how to achieve a required function more efficiently. CBA asks whether a proposed addition is justified at all. Used together, a gap is first confirmed against the project purpose, then options are generated, then each is priced and compared.

Worked example: the clinic brief requires wheelchair access. Step 1: confirm the requirement in the brief and the accessibility rules that apply. Step 2: the drawings show a step at the entrance, so the gap is a missing accessible route. Step 3: list options, such as a ramp, a lift, or regrading the entrance approach. Step 4: estimate each option's cost and its benefits, including compliance and avoided redesign. Step 5: choose the option whose benefit justifies its cost, then record the decision as a scope change.

Common mistake: pricing the cheapest option without checking that it still meets the requirement, so the gap reopens later as rework.

Consequence: an unrecorded scope change means the cost estimate, schedule and contract no longer match the work being built, and the mismatch surfaces as disputes at handover.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank's brief requires its cold store to hold 4 degrees C through a 12-hour grid outage. The drawings show a cold room but no backup power connected to it, so the gap is missing standby power for the cold room. Options listed: connect the cold room to the building's existing generator circuit, install a dedicated standby unit, or add thermal storage panels. The next step is to estimate the cost of each option and the benefits it returns over the store's life, including avoided spoilage losses, then compare them. Which action completes this step?
choices: Estimate each option's cost and the benefits it returns, then compare them against each other
Record the generator connection as a scope change before pricing any of the three options
Reduce the outage requirement to 4 hours so the cheapest option qualifies without owner approval
Adopt the cheapest option immediately, since any option that meets the brief will do
questions.why: Once options are listed, the cost-benefit step prices each one and sets its measurable and non-measurable benefits against that cost, which is what allows a justified choice to be made.

questions.prompt: A value engineering proposal for a warehouse replaces a 150 mm structural slab with a 100 mm slab to save cost. The brief requires the floor to carry forklift loads of 5 kN/m2. What is the correct way to handle the proposal?
choices: Accept it, because a thinner slab is cheaper and VE is meant to reduce cost
Treat it as a scope reduction if the load-carrying function is lost, and check it against the brief before accepting
Accept it and note the change in the cost log only, since the drawings still show a slab
Reject all VE on the floor because any change to structure is out of scope
questions.why: The teaching text says a VE idea that removes a required function is a scope reduction and must be handled as one, so the load requirement must be checked before the proposal is accepted.

questions.prompt: A school is comparing two options to fix a recurring roof leak. Option A costs 40,000 and is expected to save 6,000 per year in repairs over the 10-year life of the roof. Option B costs 25,000 and is expected to save 2,000 per year in repairs over the same life. Ignoring any non-measurable benefits, which option is justified by cost-benefit analysis, and why?
choices: Option B, because a lower upfront cost always means the benefit exceeds the cost
Option A, because its total 10-year savings of 60,000 exceed its cost of 40,000, while Option B saves only 20,000 against 25,000
Option B, because its upfront cost is lower and it is the cheaper choice
Neither, because both options cost more than they save in the first year
questions.why: Cost-benefit analysis compares the total benefit over the asset's life with the cost, and Option A returns 60,000 against a 40,000 cost while Option B returns 20,000 against 25,000.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the difference between value engineering and cost-benefit analysis in a scope-gap review?
choices: Value engineering asks whether a proposed addition is justified at all, while cost-benefit analysis asks how to deliver a required function more cheaply
Value engineering asks how to deliver a required function more efficiently, while cost-benefit analysis asks whether a proposed addition is justified at all
Value engineering is used only after the contract is signed, while cost-benefit analysis is used only before tender
Value engineering and cost-benefit analysis both answer only whether the cheapest option should be chosen
questions.why: The teaching text states that VE asks how to achieve a required function more efficiently and CBA asks whether a proposed addition is justified, so the correct pairing is the one matching those questions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use value engineering and cost-benefit analysis to find and close a scope gap on a capital project, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on the numbers.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by confirming the gap against the project purpose and the owner's brief, because a missing item is only a gap if the outcome depends on it. Then I would run value engineering on the options that could deliver that function, asking whether each can meet the requirement more cheaply or with less risk. For the shortlisted options I would run a cost-benefit analysis, comparing the cost of each addition or change against measurable benefits such as avoided rework and compliance, plus harder-to-price benefits such as user experience. The main limit is that the result is only as good as the benefit estimates. Benefits that are hard to quantify tend to be undervalued, so I would state those assumptions openly. I would then record the chosen option as a formal scope change so the cost, schedule and contract reflect what is actually being built.
rubricPoints: Confirm the gap against the project purpose or owner brief before pricing anything
Use value engineering to find cheaper or lower-risk ways to deliver the same required function
Use cost-benefit analysis to compare the cost of each option against its measurable and non-measurable benefits
Name a limit, such as benefit estimates being uncertain or hard-to-quantify benefits being undervalued
Record the chosen option as a formal scope change so cost, schedule and contract match the work

suggested.rationale: A fictional-credits cost model would let the learner price options against benefits and see how the comparison changes with the assumptions.

lessons.plain: A governance model is the agreed set of rules that says who makes which decisions on a project, how those decisions get made, and where they are checked. On a building, road or plant project, many parties (the owner, designers, contractors, funders and regulators) each have a stake, and without clear rules, decisions drift to whoever is loudest or nearest the problem. A good model sets up forums such as steering committees and review gates, gives each approver limits on money and scope, and keeps a written record. Implementing one means turning those rules into working meetings, approval thresholds and paperwork that people actually use, so the project's outcomes improve and not just its documents.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor finds that the ground under a planned foundation is much weaker than the survey showed. Before any teaching, who do you think should decide whether to change the design and pay for it, and what would you want written down first?
lessons.teach: A governance model is the set of rules that defines decision rights: who can approve what, in which forum, under which limits, and with what record kept. Its job is to make sure important choices on a project are made by people with the authority and information to make them, and that the choices are visible afterwards. It works because construction projects spread money and risk across many parties, so unclear authority causes disputes and rework. A governance model usually combines three parts. Forums are standing meetings such as a steering committee. Gates are formal review points where work may not proceed until approval is given, for example before construction starts after design review. Thresholds are limits, often in money or schedule days, that decide which level of person must approve a change. Worked example: a road rehabilitation project has a thresholds rule. Step 1: the site engineer sees the weak ground. Step 2: the change is estimated at 40,000 units of cost, which is under the engineer's limit of 25,000 only if split, so it is logged as one item. Step 3: the item is above the limit, so it goes to the steering committee. Step 4: the committee approves the design change at the gate, and the decision is recorded with its reason. A common mistake is writing a governance model down and never using it, so approvals happen informally and the record shows nothing. In a running project this causes unapproved changes, cost overruns and owner disputes that surface months later. A governance model is only real when its thresholds, forums and records are used on every significant decision.

questions.prompt: A hospital wing fit-out has a thresholds rule. Step 1: the site foreman finds an unmarked drainage pipe under the slab where the new theatre is to go. Step 2: rerouting it is estimated to add 12 days to the programme, but the project manager's limit for schedule changes is 5 days. Step 3: because 12 days is above the project manager's limit, the change is not the project manager's to approve alone. Step 4 (missing): what must happen to the change at the board's review point, and what must be kept on record?
choices: The project manager approves it after the next weekly progress meeting, because the limit only applies to cost changes.
The foreman records the 12 days in the site diary and proceeds, since the delay is only programme time and the owner can be told at handover.
The change goes to the project board at its review point, which approves or rejects it and records the decision with its reason.
The change is split into two 6-day items so each falls under the project manager's limit, and both are approved informally by email.
questions.why: The thresholds rule sends any change above the lower person's limit to the forum at that level, and the decision must be made and recorded with its reason, so the board's approval with a written reason is the required final step.

questions.prompt: In a construction governance model, what is a gate?
choices: A formal review point where work may not proceed until approval is given.
A written list of who holds decision rights for each type of change on the project.
A standing meeting, such as a monthly steering committee, where all project decisions are discussed.
A limit, usually in money or schedule days, that decides which level of person must approve a change.
questions.why: A gate is defined in the teaching text as a formal review point where work may not proceed until approval is given, which is different from a forum (a standing meeting) or a threshold (a limit).

questions.prompt: A warehouse fit-out company wrote a governance model with forums, gates and thresholds, but the site team has been agreeing crane lift changes by phone and never logging them. What is the most likely consequence on the running project?
choices: Unapproved changes, cost overruns and owner disputes that surface months later, because nothing shows who approved what.
The thresholds automatically escalate every phone agreement to the steering committee without anyone needing to record it.
The owner is protected because the written model still counts as evidence of approval.
The governance model becomes more effective because the team is working faster without formal delays.
questions.why: The teaching text says a written model that is never used leads to informal approvals with no record, which causes unapproved changes, overruns and disputes that appear months later; the model only counts when it is actually used.

questions.prompt: A three-storey clinic project gives the project manager authority over schedule changes up to 15 days, and gives the project board authority over changes above 15 days. A structural change is estimated to add 22 days. Which level must approve it?
choices: The project manager, because schedule changes are always the project manager's responsibility.
The contractor's commercial director, because the change affects the contract programme.
The site engineer, because the design change was first identified on site.
The project board, because 22 days is above the project manager's 15-day limit.
questions.why: A threshold decides the level of person who must approve a change, and since 22 days exceeds the project manager's 15-day limit, the change must go up to the board.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a governance model on a construction project is, using one concrete decision as an example, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: A governance model on a construction project is the agreed set of rules for who decides what, in which forum, and how the decision is recorded. For example, if a supplier wants to substitute a steel grade, the model might say the site manager can approve substitutions up to a set cost, the steering committee approves anything above it, and the owner's representative signs off anything that changes the scope or the building's performance requirements. Each decision goes into a decision log with its reason and approver. The main tradeoff is speed against control. Tight thresholds and several approval layers reduce surprise costs, but they slow the site, and people may route around them when a delay is costly. So I would set the thresholds with the owner up front, review them at each gate, and check the log at each steering meeting to see whether the rules are actually being followed.
rubricPoints: Defines governance model as decision rights, forums, gates or thresholds, and records
Gives a concrete construction decision and names who approves it and where
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as speed versus control or paper governance
Explains that the model only works if it is used and the decision log is checked

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises construction governance, and explaining who decides what and why is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Scope governance is the set of rules, meetings and records a construction project uses to decide what work is included and to control any change to that work. A building job has a planned list of what gets built, drawn in documents and agreed in a contract. Without a process, a client asks for one extra room, a crew builds it, and nobody agrees on the price or the schedule impact. Scope governance decides who may approve a change, how the change is written down, and when the agreed scope is frozen. Think of it as the gatekeeping system that keeps what gets built matched to what was promised.
lessons.guessPrompt: A subcontractor on a hospital wing says a wall they were asked to build differs from the drawing, and they start building the revised version today to keep the schedule. What is the first governance problem you would see, and what would you want in place before anyone builds it?
lessons.teach:
Scope governance is the structure that decides what belongs in the project's work and how changes to that work get approved. Three terms matter. The scope baseline is the approved, frozen description of the work: the drawings, specifications, and the work breakdown structure, which is a tree that splits the total work into packages. A change request is a written proposal to alter that baseline. The change control board, often shortened to CCB, is the group with authority to approve, reject or defer change requests. On construction jobs it usually includes the owner's representative, the design lead and the contractor's project manager.

Why it works: construction scope is expensive to alter after work starts, because materials are ordered, crews are scheduled and inspections are booked. A written baseline gives everyone one reference, and a single approval path stops a verbal request from quietly becoming site work.

Worked example: a client asks to move a kitchen door on level 2. Step 1: the site lead logs a change request with the drawing reference and the reason. Step 2: the design lead estimates the impact, which here means a structural check, a revised electrical layout, and two extra days. Step 3: the CCB reviews the estimate and approves it through a change order that adjusts the cost and the completion date. Step 4: only then does the crew move the door, and the baseline is updated with the new drawing revision.

Common mistake: treating a site instruction as approval. A foreman saying 'just do it' bypasses the board, so the cost and schedule never reach the record, and at closeout nobody can show what was paid for and why.

Consequence: if the baseline drifts without being recorded, the final inspection tests the building against drawings that no longer match it, and the owner can refuse acceptance.

questions.prompt: A school extension team wants to swap a classroom window from single to double glazing. Step 1: the site engineer logs a change request with the drawing reference and the reason, which is improved insulation. Step 2: the design lead estimates the impact: a revised glazing schedule, a heavier lintel check, and three extra days. Step 3 is missing from this trace. Step 4: only after that step does the crew install the new windows, and the baseline is updated with the new drawing revision. What belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: The change control board reviews the estimate and approves it through a change order that adjusts cost and completion date.
The contractor's project manager alone signs off, since the change is small and inside the same trade.
The site engineer and the foreman agree the swap verbally so the crew can start the next morning.
The crew installs the windows first and the cost is recorded at the end of the month.
questions.why: The change control board is the group with authority to approve changes, and approval through a change order is what records the cost and date impact before the work proceeds.

questions.prompt: In construction scope governance, what is the scope baseline?
choices: The approved, frozen description of the work, including drawings, specifications and the work breakdown structure.
The monthly cost forecast that the owner's finance team reviews.
The list of subcontractor bids received before the contract was signed.
A running daily log of site progress and weather delays kept by the superintendent.
questions.why: The baseline is defined in the teaching text as the approved, frozen description of the work, made up of drawings, specifications and the work breakdown structure.

questions.prompt: On a warehouse job, a superintendent agreed by phone with the owner's representative to move a loading dock three metres. No change request was logged and the change control board never saw it. What is the governance gap, and what risk does it create?
choices: The phone call is valid because the owner's representative approved it, so the only gap is missing paperwork for the crew.
The change is fine as long as the drawings are redrawn later, since the baseline is updated after the work.
The change bypassed the board, so its cost and schedule never reach the record, and at closeout nobody can show what was paid for and why.
The gap is only that the foreman lacked a permit, which the inspector will catch before closeout.
questions.why: A verbal instruction that skips the single approval path keeps cost and schedule impacts out of the record, which is the consequence the teaching text describes for site instructions treated as approval.

questions.prompt: A hospital renovation has a pending request to defer a change until after the next inspection. Which group has the authority to make that decision?
choices: The contractor's accounts team, because deferral affects the payment schedule.
The structural engineer of record working alone, because the change touches a load-bearing element.
The change control board, which typically includes the owner's representative, the design lead and the contractor's project manager.
The site foreman, because deferral is a scheduling matter on the ground.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the change control board as the group with authority to approve, reject or defer change requests, and names its usual membership.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to construction how a scope change should be handled on a live job. Name the structure that approves it and at least one limit or tradeoff of the process.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd tell them the baseline is the frozen set of drawings, specs and the work breakdown structure that the contract refers to, and any change to it goes through the change control board, not the site. The site lead raises a change request with the drawing reference and reason. The design lead and cost estimator assess the impact on design, cost and schedule. The board decides to approve, reject or defer, and an approved change becomes a change order that updates price and completion date before any work starts. The tradeoff is speed: the process adds days to small fixes, so teams sometimes batch minor changes or set a dollar threshold for quicker approval. That threshold has to be written down, or the process erodes back into verbal instructions. Changes the board never sees are the main risk.
rubricPoints: Names the scope baseline as the reference that every change is measured against.
Names the change control board as the approving body and the change request as its input.
Explains that an approved change becomes a change order that adjusts cost and schedule before work starts.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as approval delay or the risk of informal site changes.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a live change request on a construction site adds the most, because exam questions ask which structure applies at a specific decision point.

scenarios.title: Ferncliff Outpatient Wing: Change, Claim, and Interface Points
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Civil Works is a fictional mid-sized general contractor. It is building a three-storey outpatient wing for a fictional client, Ferncliff Health, under a design-build contract. In design-build, one party (here Brightwater) takes responsibility for both the design and the construction, so the contractor and designer share one set of obligations. You are the newly appointed project manager, and you are reviewing three items in the project log before the monthly owner meeting.

Item A: Ferncliff's facilities director asked, in an email, for the level 2 treatment rooms to be moved two metres east to suit new equipment. The design team has sized the change and Brightwater has priced it. A change order is a written instruction that changes scope, price, or time within the existing contract, and both parties sign it. A claim is a formal demand by one party for money or time that it believes the contract entitles it to, usually raised when the parties disagree.

Item B: Brightwater's subcontractor for finishes says it lost 14 days because Ferncliff took three weeks to approve a tile selection. The subcontractor has sent a notice saying it intends to claim the time and cost. A notice is a formal written warning that a right may be pursued, and it usually starts a time limit under the contract.

Item C: A supplier has offered to deliver structural steel for level 3 about four weeks early if the order is placed this week, at a small premium. This is a positive risk, meaning an uncertain event that would help the project if it happened. The team had not logged it. Your team also ran a Monte Carlo simulation earlier, which means running thousands of random trials using a range of likely durations for each activity, to estimate how likely the project is to finish by its target date. Its result showed a 58 percent chance of finishing on time. A risk register is the living list of risks, with an owner, a likelihood, an impact, and a planned response for each.

The owner meeting is in two days. Complete the three tasks below.

1. For Item A and Item B, decide whether each is a change order or a claim, and state the first step you would take on each to keep the project moving and protect the contract position.

2. For Item C, explain how you would record this opportunity in the risk register and whether you would recommend acting on it, referring to what the Monte Carlo result tells you.

3. Level 2 has ductwork from the mechanical package running through the same ceiling zone as the structural steel beams, so the two packages must agree where they meet. Explain what an interface point is and describe how you would plan the one for this ceiling zone, including who must agree and when.
subParts: Classify Items A and B as change order or claim and state the first step for each
Record the positive risk in Item C and recommend action using the Monte Carlo result
Plan the interface point between the mechanical ductwork and structural steel at level 2
modelAnswer: Item A is a change order. It is a scope change the owner is requesting, it has been designed and priced, and both parties can sign it. The first step is to issue a written change order request that states the revised scope, the price, and any time impact, then obtain both signatures before the work is done. Item B is a claim, because the subcontractor is asserting entitlement to time and money for a delay it blames on the owner, and the parties have not yet agreed. The first step is to acknowledge the notice in writing within the contract time limit, without admitting liability, and to ask for the supporting records such as the approval request dates and the impacted activity. Acknowledging in time protects the contract position, because a missed notice deadline can weaken or lose a claim.

Log the steel early delivery as a positive risk in the register, with a description (supplier can deliver level 3 steel about four weeks early for a small premium), an owner (procurement lead), a likelihood estimate, a benefit estimate in time and money, and a response such as accept and pursue or enhance. Recommend action by comparing the premium cost against the value of the time gained. The Monte Carlo result shows only a 58 percent chance of finishing on time, so the schedule has real exposure. Because the four-week gain would move the probability of meeting the target upward, the recommendation is to place the order this week, provided the premium is small compared with the expected value of reduced delay, and to rerun the simulation with the new durations to confirm the improvement.

An interface point is a defined place or boundary where two work packages must physically or functionally connect, and where each side's responsibility must be agreed. Here, the mechanical ductwork and the structural beams share a ceiling zone, so the mechanical and structural packages must agree on clearances, beam penetrations, and who supports the duct hangers. The plan should name the owner of the interface (the design-build lead, with both package managers as contributors), set a date before the steel is erected, and require coordinated drawings or a clash check showing the duct and beam positions. Sign-off happens when both packages confirm the agreed clearances in writing. The common mistake is to leave this to the site crews, who then discover clashes during installation and create rework and delay.

scenarios.title: Harbor Line Parking Structure: Conflicting Schedule Updates
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Line Builders is a fictional general contractor building a four-level parking structure for a city transit authority. Three weeks ago, the electrical subcontractor moved its conduit rough-in from week 12 to week 16 because of a late switchgear delivery. The change was made in a spreadsheet kept by the subcontractor's project engineer and was mentioned in a phone call to the site superintendent. The owner's representative, the structural engineer, and the design team were never told. Last week the owner's representative sent an email asking why the concrete pour schedule still assumed electrical work in week 12, and the superintendent had to admit he did not know the date had changed. Two inspection bookings were made on the wrong dates, and the owner now doubts the team's control of the schedule. Harbor Line's project manager, Ana Ruiz, must respond. Using the unit's tools, answer the following:

1. Identify which tool should hold the single current version of the schedule and related dated commitments, define it in plain terms, and explain why it is better here than the spreadsheet and phone call.

2. Propose a short recurring cross-team meeting in the style of an Obeya or Big Room, where the visual wall shows all trades and the owner's team. Name one pitfall of that practice that Ana should avoid in this project.

3. Explain how Commitment-based Management (CbM), where each subcontractor makes a dated promise each week and the team tracks whether promises are kept, would catch a problem like this earlier, and state what the reliability measure would show.
subParts: Identify the tool, define it, and justify it over the spreadsheet and phone call
Propose an Obeya or Big Room session and name one pitfall to avoid
Explain how CbM would catch the problem earlier and what reliability shows
modelAnswer: The correct tool is the project management information system (PMIS), which is a shared software record that stores project data such as schedules, document logs, and dated commitments in one place that everyone with permission can see. It holds a single version of the truth, so when the electrical date changes, the change is entered once and the owner, design team, and superintendent see the same date. A spreadsheet on one engineer's computer and a phone call leave no shared record, no change history, and no notice to people who depend on the date. A good answer names a PMIS, explains it as a shared, versioned record, and contrasts it with the local spreadsheet and verbal update.

A reasonable proposal is a weekly 45-minute session at a visual wall or shared board, held in a room with the superintendent, the electrical and concrete leads, inspection coordination, and an owner representative. Each trade posts its look-ahead dates, and the wall shows the schedule in one view so conflicts appear as physical gaps. A common pitfall is treating the wall as a status report to be read rather than a decision forum, so the room fills with updates and nobody resolves the switchgear and pour conflict. Another valid pitfall is inviting people who cannot make decisions, or letting the owner's team attend without authority to accept changes. The answer should name one pitfall and tie it to this project.

CbM is a method where each subcontractor makes specific, dated weekly commitments, such as I will have conduit rough-in complete by Friday, and the team records whether each promise was kept. In this case, the electrical subcontractor would have had to commit to a date every week, so the slip from week 12 to week 16 would have appeared as a broken or revised promise in the first week it became real, not three weeks later. The reliability measure is the percentage of commitments kept each week, for example 6 of 8 kept is 75 percent. A low or falling reliability score signals hidden constraints, such as the switchgear delay, before the owner finds them. The answer should explain the weekly promise and the reliability percentage, and note that the early signal lets the team act sooner.

scenarios.title: Shielding request mid-fit-out at a medical office building
scenarios.scenario: Ostrander Build Co. is a fictional general contractor building a three-storey medical office building for Calder Health Partners, also fictional. The structure is finished and fit-out (interior walls, ceilings, and equipment rooms) has started. Eight weeks in, the owner's operations lead asks for radiation shielding in one room so it can house a digital X-ray unit. The contract's scope document, called the scope baseline (the agreed description of what the project will deliver, against which every later change is measured), lists a standard exam room with ordinary gypsum board walls and no shielding. Shielding means dense lining in walls, floor, or ceiling that blocks radiation. A change order is the formal written record that changes scope, cost, or schedule, and it should be approved before the extra work is done. Value engineering means reviewing a design for a way to deliver the same needed function at lower cost or risk. Cost-benefit analysis compares the expected gains of a choice against its total cost. Two options are on the table. Lead-lined gypsum board is estimated at 42,000 with a two-week lead time. A steel-plate and concrete option is estimated at 61,000 with a five-week lead time. The fit-out subcontractor's schedule locks in three days, and the company logs requests, estimates, and approvals in a shared online change-order platform. As the project manager, respond to the owner with a plan, not a simple yes or no. 1. Decide whether this request is a scope change or a scope gap, restate the outcome the owner needs, and explain how the scope baseline should be revised. 2. Propose when the change order should be raised and a fast approval process that fits the three-day window, stating what must be signed off before work starts and what can proceed in the meantime. 3. Compare the two shielding options using cost-benefit analysis and value engineering, recommend one, and name one benefit and one downside of recording this change on the shared platform.
subParts: Scope change or gap, outcome, and baseline revision
Change-order timing and rapid approval process
Option comparison, recommendation, and platform trade-off
modelAnswer: This is a scope change, not a gap in the design: the owner has added a requirement after the baseline was agreed, so the design team did not miss it, it was never in scope. Restate the outcome as a room that can safely house and operate a digital X-ray unit and meets radiation safety requirements, not as 'add lead lining'. The scope baseline should be revised by formally adding the shielded exam room, its performance requirement, the chosen material, and the resulting cost and schedule impact, with the owner's approval recorded. The original baseline should be kept unchanged so the history of the change stays visible.

Raise the change order now, before the subcontractor's schedule locks, rather than waiting for the full estimate or the owner's final decision on material. Use a fast track: send the draft change order with both options and their estimates to the owner's representative and design lead within the first day, request sign-off on the outcome and budget envelope within the second day, and confirm the chosen option in writing by the third. Before any shielding work starts, the signed change order, the revised drawings for the room, and the radiation consultant's confirmation must be on file. Non-affected work in other rooms can proceed in the meantime, and the subcontractor should be told the room's start date is provisional.

Compare the options on total cost, schedule effect, and whether they meet the performance need. Lead-lined board costs less and finishes two weeks sooner, but it may need a specialist check for coverage and joins. Steel-plate and concrete costs about 19,000 more and adds three extra weeks, but it may be simpler to verify. Recommend the option that meets the radiation requirement at the lower total cost and schedule effect, and show the calculation, for example: the cheaper option saves 19,000 and two weeks, provided the consultant confirms it meets the requirement. A proper value engineering review asks whether the cheaper option delivers the same function, not merely whether it is cheaper. On the platform, a benefit is a single traceable record of who requested what, when it was estimated, and who approved it. A downside is that a platform makes the record look authoritative, so a wrong estimate or an unsigned draft can be treated as approved if users do not check the status field.

scenarios.title: Mid-build scope request at a medical office project
scenarios.scenario: Harrow Ridge Builders, a fictional general contractor, is six months into building a four-storey medical office for a client called Lakeview Health. The project manager, Dana, is new to the role. A Lakeview facilities manager emails the site foreman asking for a larger rooftop mechanical screen so it hides new air-handling units, and says the change is 'small and should be quick.' The foreman has started ordering materials based on that email. Dana has to decide how the request should be handled. Terms used here: a scope baseline is the approved, agreed description of what the project will deliver, including its approved drawings and specifications, and a change control board (CCB) is a standing group with authority to approve, reject, or defer changes to that baseline. A decision log is a dated record of each governance decision, who made it, and why. Answer the following: 1. Name the governance structure that should receive this request, and state what it is responsible for doing with it. 2. Name the document the request must be checked against, and explain what that check establishes before any work proceeds. 3. Describe the practice that should record the outcome and link it to the contract, including what must happen if the change is approved.
subParts: Name the governance structure that should receive the request and its responsibility
Name the baseline document to check against and what the check establishes
Describe the recording practice and contract link if the change is approved
modelAnswer: The request should go to the change control board (CCB), a standing group with authority to approve, reject, or defer changes to the scope baseline. Its responsibility is to review the request formally, assess its effect on scope, cost, and schedule, and decide before any work on the change starts. A single email to a foreman does not count as a governance decision, so the foreman should pause ordering and route the request to the CCB.

The request must be checked against the approved scope baseline, meaning the signed-off drawings, specifications, and scope statement for the rooftop screen. The check establishes whether the request is actually a change (it departs from what was approved) and how large the departure is in terms of area, materials, structure, and schedule. Without this comparison, the team cannot judge whether the request is small or whether it affects the building's structural or mechanical design.

The outcome should be recorded in the decision log with the date, the requester, the CCB members who decided, the reasons, and the approved cost and schedule impact. If approved, the change should be issued as a formal change order or change directive under the construction contract, so the price, time, and responsibility for the extra work are agreed in writing before construction. The updated drawings should then be issued and the scope baseline revised under version control, so everyone builds from the same approved documents.
